Based on experimental hardware test results, a code that models the relationship between the EV state of charge and charging power for different EV and EVSE types was developed and deployed on the CHIL devices. For the purposes of this demonstration, this code is referred to as the transfer function. In addition to active power, the transfer function also calculates reactive power consumption as a function of SOC, as well as the efficiency curve of the charging equipment. The efficiency curve is included to account for power losses in the chargers’ converters, thereby improving the accuracy of the power system model. The energy delivered to the vehicle is calculated within the transfer function in real time, and SOC updates are derived based on the vehicle’s battery capacity. Each CHIL device connects to the Real-Time Digital Simulator (RTDS), a high-performance computing platform used to model power systems in real time. RTDS simulations are developed and executed through RSCAD, the companion software environment that provides the interface for building, running, and monitoring real-time models. Communication between the CHIL devices and the RTDS is implemented using TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) or UDP (User Datagram Protocol). In parallel, each CHIL device communicates with the SCM using OCPP. OCPP, developed by the Open Charge Alliance, is an open communication standard that enables interoperability between EV charging stations and central management systems from different vendors. In this project, each CHIL device adopts the OCPP 26 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. v1.6J protocol to emulate a charging station. The OCPP package used to implement the OCPP protocol is based on Python programming language.1 In addition to the CHIL devices, hardware chargers are included in the test bed for PHIL validation. Two physical chargers are available for this purpose: one rated at 350 kW and another at 25 kW. Similar to the CHIL devices, the hardware chargers communicate with the SCM via OCPP v1.6J. Node-RED: A flow-based programming tool, originally developed by IBM and now part of the OpenJS Foundation. Within the test bed, it serves as the central integration platform, enabling seamless communication between the SCM and other devices. Node- RED hosts the OCPP server for CHIL devices, manages UDP sockets for interaction with RSCAD, and uses MQTT as the backbone protocol for data exchange with the SCM. 2. MQTT: A lightweight, publish-subscribe messaging protocol designed to exchange messages between devices in the Internet of Things environment. Devices like the OCPP server or SCM can publish data, such as measurements, feedback signals, or control commands, to a specific topic.
